abstract:
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a potentially life-threatening cardiovascular condition. However, the role of limb-specific fat distribution and its associated metabolomic signatures in VTE remains unclear.
To assess associations between upper- and lower-limb fat distribution and VTE risk and to evaluate whether circulating metabolites mediate these relationships.
This retrospective cohort study analyzed UK Biobank data, in which arm and leg fat mass were measured by bioelectrical impedance. Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines assessed sex-specific associations with incident VTE, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was used to identify metabolites associated with arm-to-leg fat mass percentage, followed by mediation analyses.
Over a median follow-up of 13.6 years, 14 593 VTE events occurred among 458 651 participants. A higher arm-to-leg fat mass percentage was associated with increased VTE risk, with hazard ratios of 1.81 (95% CI, 1.63-2.00) in women and 1.55 (95% CI, 1.47-1.64) in men when comparing the highest tertile with the lowest. A total of 138 metabolites in women and 38 in men were associated with arm-to-leg fat distribution. In women, the metabolomic signature mediated 15.2% (95% CI, 6.8%-21.9%) of the association between arm-to-leg fat and VTE and 21.1% (95% CI, 12.8%-28.4%) of the corresponding association with pulmonary embolism; no significant mediation was observed in men.
Predominant upper peripheral fat distribution is associated with a high risk of VTE. Sex-specific metabolomic signatures partially mediate these associations in women, underscoring the importance of integrating limb fat distribution with metabolomics to improve VTE risk assessment.
